blocks.title: A familiar road-rider problem
blocks.content:
On pavement, you can get away with holding one position for a long time. The first stretch of washboard or scattered stones asks more of you. If your arms are straight and your hands are bearing your weight, every small change in the ground feels like a steering input. You may grip harder and look down at the front tire.

You do not need to ride that section faster to fix it. Start on easier ground and give the bike room to move under you.

blocks.label: A position you can adjust
blocks.content:
Keep your hands on the hoods with your fingers able to reach the brakes. Bend your elbows enough that they can move. Support some of your weight through your feet; keep your knees soft. Let your hips move at the hip joints while your back stays in a comfortable, neutral range.

There is no fixed head height to hold. Look where you want to ride and notice whether you can steer without bracing against the bars.

blocks.title: Gravel God: rider position on easy gravel
blocks.alt: Illustrated Gravel God rider shown from the side and three-quarter view, with both hands on the hoods, bent elbows, and feet on the pedals.
blocks.caption: Illustrated posture reference. Watch the hands, elbows, and feet. Practice the position at a pace that lets you steer and brake comfortably; the animation is not a demonstration of tire grip or bump absorption.

blocks.content:
Your arms and legs can make small adjustments while the bike rolls over uneven ground. Start by removing the pressure from your hands that makes those adjustments hard. Keep both hands where you can brake. Bend your elbows and knees without dropping into a deep squat or folding your back.

A hip hinge means bending at the hips. It does not mean repeatedly bending your lower spine to absorb bumps. On rougher ground you may briefly take some weight off the saddle so your legs have room to move. Sit back down when the surface settles. If the bike is bouncing you around, lower your speed or choose a smoother line.
Use the Lesson 1 check when you notice pressure in your hands. Slow down, put some support through your feet, and let your elbows bend. Keep the brake levers within reach.

blocks.title: Set up an adjustable position
blocks.description: Use this check on a quiet, mostly flat gravel road before you try rougher sections.

steps.detail: Choose a clear line with room to stop. Keep both hands on the hoods and cover the brakes as needed.
Let your elbows and knees bend a little. Check that you can still steer and pedal without straining.
Tip forward gently at the hip joints while keeping your back comfortable. Do not force a lower position or try to hold your head perfectly still.
On small bumps, let your arms and legs move. For a rough patch, coast if that gives you better control and take a little weight off the saddle. Slow down or stop if the bike feels unpredictable.

blocks.content: On a long gravel ride or in a race, use the same position check before a rough section: look for a clear line, reduce speed while the surface is predictable, then let your arms and legs move when the bumps arrive. If you cannot see a line through it, riding around or walking the section is a sound choice.

blocks.title: Easy-gravel position check
blocks.description: Repeat a short, visible section of smooth gravel. Compare how steering feels when you brace on the bars and when your arms and legs can move. Do not seek out washboard for this first practice.

variants.label: Flat, quiet gravel at an easy pace
steps: Pick a short, open section with no traffic or blind corners. Walk it first if you are unsure of the surface.
Ride through at a pace where you can talk and stop comfortably. Notice where your weight rests: saddle, feet, and hands.
On the next pass, keep both hands on the hoods, bend your elbows and knees slightly, and look ahead along your chosen line.
Try one pass coasting and one with light pedaling. If either feels unstable, slow down or return to smoother ground.
After each pass, stop and note one change in steering or comfort. Keep the version that gives you more room to respond.

variants.label: Add a mildly uneven section after the first drill feels controlled
steps: Choose a familiar section with a few small bumps and a clear runout. Stay at an easy pace.
Keep your hands on the hoods and your eyes on the line ahead. Let your knees and elbows move as the bike rolls over the bumps.
Try seated pedaling, then coasting with a little weight off the saddle. Notice which position lets you steer and brake more easily.
Stop if you lose a clear line, need to brace on the bars, or feel pain. Return to the easy section before repeating.

proof_gate.description: On familiar easy gravel, you can keep both hands at the brakes, look ahead, and steer without bracing on the bars.
proof_gate.target: Describe the position and repeat it at a comfortable pace on a clear, low-traffic section.

blocks.content:
### If the position feels wrong

**Your hands are carrying your weight.** Slow down and check that your feet share the load. Bend your elbows without letting go of the hoods.

**Your back feels strained.** Come out of the hinge and use a position that feels comfortable. A bike-fit or health professional can help if pain persists.

**The bike still feels unsettled.** Choose a smoother line and a lower speed. Position gives you room to respond; it does not make every surface rideable.

blocks.question: What should you change first if small bumps make you brace against the handlebars?

options.text: Speed up so the bumps pass more quickly
Slow down, keep both hands near the brakes, and let your elbows and knees bend
Lock your elbows to hold the front wheel straight
Take both hands off the bars to relax your shoulders

blocks.explanation: An easy pace, reachable brakes, and joints that can move give you more control. If that does not feel stable, choose smoother ground.

blocks.content: Before Lesson 3, repeat the easy-gravel position check. Write down where you felt pressure through your hands and which adjustment made steering easier.
Next, look at tire pressure and traction. Start with your tire and rim limits, then use notes from familiar rides to learn how your setup feels on different surfaces.
